title: Unit Launch - Rule-Based vs Learning Systems
summary: Students meet the term's big question by sorting three real systems into 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from data', posting their own questions and helping agree the class responsible-use rules.
objectives: Generate at least two questions about how rule-based and learning systems differ.
Classify three systems as 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from data', justifying each.
Co-construct the unit success criteria and the responsible-use norms for AI tools.

body: Some machines are told every single step. Others are shown lots of examples and work out the pattern themselves. This term you become a system detective - can you tell which kind you are looking at?

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can ask at least two genuine questions about rule-based and learning systems.
I can sort three systems into 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from data' and give a reason for each.
I can help write our class responsible-use rules for AI tools.

terms.definition: A system that follows fixed steps a person wrote for it.
A system that finds patterns from many examples instead of fixed rules.
The examples or information a learning system is shown.
The pattern a learning system builds from its data.
One piece of data, like one photo or one email.

sections.heading: Two kinds of machine
body: A [[rule-based system]] is like a recipe. A person writes every step, and the machine follows them exactly. A Salik toll gate charges you when your car passes - a person set that rule.

A [[learning system]] is different. Nobody writes a rule for every case. Instead it is shown many examples - this is [[data]] - and it finds the pattern by itself. The pattern it builds is called a [[model]].

sections.label: The distinction the whole unit rests on
sections.heading: Where did the rule come from?
sections.altText: Two columns. In a rule-based machine a person writes the rule and the machine follows it. In a learning machine, examples go in and the machine works the rule out for itself.

left.title: Rule-based machine
steps: A person works out the rule
They write it down as steps

right.title: Learning machine
steps: The machine finds the rule in them
The machine uses what it found

sections.caption: Same job, different source. Ask **who worked out the rule** — that is the question this unit keeps coming back to.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: If you know which kind a system is, you can guess when it might fail. A rule-based system fails when something happens that has no rule. A learning system can fail if it was shown poor or unfair examples.
Neither kind is magic, and neither understands like a person. That is why we always check what a machine tells us.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Time to be a detective. Sort three systems, then post the questions you most want answered this term.
items: Watch the two clips your teacher shows and spot which machine was told every step.
Sort the three cards into 'fixed rules' or 'learns from data'.
Write a reason under each card.
Post two questions on the class question wall.
Help agree one class rule for safe AI use.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which system was hardest to sort, and why?
What is one clue that a system learned from examples?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write one thing you now understand about how machines make decisions.
Write one question you still have.

worksheet.title: Week 1 - Core - Worksheet | Unit Launch - Rule-Based vs Learning Systems

questions.prompt: A spam filter was built by showing a computer thousands of emails that people had already labelled 'spam' or 'not spam'. Nobody wrote a rule for every email. Which sorting and reason is correct?

options.text: Learns from data, because it found the pattern itself from many labelled example emails.
Follows fixed rules, because a person had to label the example emails first.
Learns from data, because it gets faster the more emails you send it.
Follows fixed rules, because a person wrote a step for every kind of email it might meet.

feedback.correct: Right - the logic came from the examples, not from steps a person wrote, which is exactly what makes it a learning system.
feedback.incorrect: People labelled the examples, but nobody wrote a rule for each email - the filter found the pattern in that data itself, so it learns from data.

questions.prompt: A photo app was shown 10,000 photos that people had already labelled 'cat' or 'not cat', and it worked out the pattern for itself. A Salik toll gate charges every car that passes, because a person wrote that step. Match each part of the story to the word that names it.

left.text: The 10,000 labelled photos the app was shown
One single labelled photo out of that collection
The pattern the app built so it can spot cats in photos it has never seen
The toll gate, which charges every car because a person wrote that step

feedback.correct: Good - you used the words on a real case: many examples make up the data, the pattern built from them is the model, and written steps make a rule-based system.
feedback.incorrect: The whole collection shown to the app is the data, one photo from it is an example, the pattern built from them is the model, and the toll gate with its written step is the rule-based system.

questions.prompt: You want to work out whether a new app follows fixed rules or learns from data. Which questions would actually help you decide? Choose all that would help.

options.text: Was it shown lots of examples that people had already labelled?
Did a person write a step for every case the app has to handle?
Would the app behave differently if it had been shown different examples?
How quickly does the app give you an answer?
Which company made the app, and how new is it?

feedback.correct: Yes - good questions go after where the logic came from: written steps, or a pattern found in examples.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and who made it are the same for both kinds. The useful questions ask where the logic came from - written steps, or examples the app learned a pattern from.

questions.prompt: True or false? A learning system is really just a very long list of fixed rules that a programmer typed in, one rule for every case.

feedback.correct: Correct - no one types a rule for every case; the system is shown many examples and builds the pattern itself.
feedback.incorrect: That is the common mix-up. A learning system has no written rule for each case - it finds the pattern from the examples it is shown.

questions.prompt: Fill in each gap with either 'follows fixed rules' or 'learns from data'. A toll gate charges every car as it passes, because a person wrote that step for it, so it ___(1). A spam filter was shown thousands of emails already labelled spam or not spam and worked out the pattern itself, so it ___(2).

feedback.correct: Well sorted - you used the deciding clue each time: who supplied the logic, a person or the examples.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who supplied the logic. A person wrote the toll gate's step, so it follows fixed rules; the filter found its own pattern in the examples, so it learns from data.

formative.targets: Baseline for the rule-based vs learning-system distinction and safe-use norms
formative.check: Diagnostic KWL + question wall + rule/learning sort (not graded)
formative.successCriteria: Poses at least 2 genuine questions and sorts at least 2 of 3 systems with a reason.
formative.evidence: Sorted systems + question wall on the baseline sheet.
